blocks.p: Now you may well suppose that long before this, word had been carried by someone or other to the good King Shaddai of how his Mansoul, in the continent of Universe, was lost, and how the renegade giant Diabolus, once one of His Majesty’s own servants, had rebelled against the King and seized it for himself. Yes, the news reached the King in every detail.

First, how Diabolus had come upon Mansoul, a simple and innocent people, with craft, cunning, lies, and deceit. Next, that he had treacherously killed their right noble and valiant captain, Captain Resistance, as he stood on the gate with the rest of the townsmen. Next, how my brave Lord Innocent had fallen down dead (of grief, some say; others say from being poisoned by the stinking breath of one Mr. Dwell-on-it) on hearing his just lord and rightful prince, Shaddai, so abused by the mouth of so filthy a Diabolonian as that scoundrel Dwell-on-it. The messenger told further that after Dwell-on-it had made a short speech to the townsmen on behalf of his master Diabolus, the simple town, believing what was said, had with one consent opened Ear-gate, the chief gate of the town, and let him and his crew in to take possession of the famous town of Mansoul. He showed, too, how Diabolus had dealt with the Lord Mayor, my Lord Understanding, and with the Recorder, Mr. Conscience: he had put them out of every place of power and trust. He showed also that my Lord Willbewill had turned an outright rebel and renegade, and so had one Mr. Mind, his clerk; and that the two of them roamed and reveled all over the town, teaching the wicked their ways. He said, moreover, that Diabolus had put this Willbewill in great trust, and in particular had given all the strongholds of Mansoul into his hands, and that Mr. Affection had been made my Lord Willbewill’s deputy in his most rebellious business.
“Yes,” said the messenger, “this monster, Lord Willbewill, has openly disowned his King Shaddai, and has horribly given his faith and pledged his word to Diabolus.”

“And besides all this,” said the messenger, “the new king, or rather the rebel tyrant over the once famous but now perishing town of Mansoul, has set up a Lord Mayor and a Recorder of his own. For Lord Mayor he has set up one Mr. Lustings, and for Recorder, Mr. Forget-Good: two of the vilest men in all the town of Mansoul.”

This faithful messenger went on to tell what sort of new aldermen Diabolus had made, and that he had built several strong forts, towers, and strongholds in Mansoul. He told also, and I had almost forgotten this, how Diabolus had put the town of Mansoul under arms, the better to equip them to resist Shaddai their King on his behalf, should he come to bring them back to their former obedience.

Now this bearer of tidings did not give his account in private, but in open court, with the King and his Son, the high lords, chief captains, and nobles all present to hear. And by the time they had heard the whole story, it would have amazed anyone who had been there to see what sorrow and grief and anguish of spirit there was among all ranks, to think that famous Mansoul was taken. Only the King and his Son had foreseen all this long before; yes, and had made ample provision for the relief of Mansoul, though they did not tell everyone so. Yet because they too would share in mourning the misery of Mansoul, they also lamented its loss, and that in the highest degree. The King said plainly that it grieved him to the heart, and you may be sure his Son was not one bit behind him. So they convinced everyone around them that they had love and compassion for the famous town of Mansoul.

Well, when the King and his Son had withdrawn into the private chamber, they consulted again about what they had planned before: namely, that as Mansoul would in time be permitted to be lost, so it should just as certainly be recovered again; recovered, I say, in such a way that both the King and his Son would win eternal fame and glory by it. So after this consultation, the Son of Shaddai (a sweet and gracious person, one who always had great tenderness for those in affliction, but who had deadly enmity in his heart against Diabolus, both because he was appointed to it and because Diabolus sought his crown and dignity), this Son of Shaddai, I say, having struck hands with his Father and promised that he would be his servant to recover his Mansoul again, stood by his resolution and would not go back on it. The substance of their agreement was this: that at a certain time, fixed by them both, the King’s Son would make a journey into the country of Universe, and there, in a way that satisfied justice and equity, by making amends for the follies of Mansoul, he would lay the foundation of its perfect deliverance from Diabolus and from his tyranny.

Moreover, Emmanuel (for that was the Son’s name, and it means “God with us”) resolved to make war, at a fitting time, on the giant Diabolus, even while he held the town of Mansoul; and fairly, by strength of hand, to drive him out of his hold, his nest, and take it for his own dwelling.

When this had been resolved, orders were given to the Lord Chief Secretary, the King’s own Secretary, who knows his mind, to draw up a fair record of what had been decided, and to have it published in every corner of the kingdom of Universe. A short summary of its contents you may take here, if you please:

Let all who are concerned know that the Son of Shaddai, the great King, is bound by covenant to his Father to bring his Mansoul back to him again; yes, and through the power of his matchless love, to put Mansoul into a far better and happier condition than it was in before Diabolus took it.
These papers were published in many places, to the no small annoyance of the tyrant Diabolus. “For now,” he thought, “I shall be harassed, and my dwelling will be taken from me.”

But when this matter, I mean this purpose of the King and his Son, first got about at court, who can describe how the high lords, chief captains, and noble princes there were taken with it! First they whispered it to one another, and then it began to ring out through the King’s palace, everyone marveling at the glorious design that the King and his Son had set on foot for the miserable town of Mansoul. Indeed, the courtiers could scarcely do anything for the King or the kingdom without mixing in some word of the love the King and his Son had for Mansoul.

Nor could these lords, high captains, and princes be content to keep the news at court. Before the records were even finished, they came down themselves and told it in Universe. At last, as I said, it reached the ears of Diabolus, to his no small displeasure; for you may imagine it would trouble him to hear of such a design against him. Well, after turning it over a few times in his mind, he settled on these four things.

First, that this news, these good tidings, should if possible be kept from the ears of Mansoul. “For,” he said, “if they once come to know that Shaddai, their former King, and Emmanuel his Son are planning good for the town of Mansoul, what can I expect but that Mansoul will revolt from under my hand and government and return to him again?”
To accomplish this, he renewed his flattery of my Lord Willbewill, and gave him strict charge and command to keep watch day and night at all the gates of the town, especially Ear-gate and Eye-gate.

“For I hear of a design,” he said, “a design to make traitors of us all, and to bring Mansoul back into its first bondage. I hope these are only flying rumors. Even so, on no account let any such news into Mansoul, or the people will be disheartened by it. It can be no welcome news to you, my lord; I am sure it is none to me; and at this time all our wisdom and care should go into nipping in the bud every rumor that tends to trouble our people. So, my lord, do as I say in this matter. Let strong guards be kept daily at every gate of the town. Stop and examine any who come from far away to trade, and admit none of them into Mansoul unless they plainly favor our excellent government. I command, moreover,” said Diabolus, “that spies walk continually up and down the town of Mansoul, with power to suppress and destroy any they find plotting against us, or chattering about what Shaddai and Emmanuel intend.”

This was done accordingly. My Lord Willbewill listened to his lord and master, went willingly after his commandment, and with all diligence kept anyone from going out, and anyone who tried to bring these tidings from coming into the town.

Second, when this was done, Diabolus, to make Mansoul as secure as he could, framed and imposed on the townsfolk a new oath and a horrible covenant: namely, that they would never desert him or his government, nor betray him, nor seek to change his laws; but would own, confess, stand by, and acknowledge him as their rightful king, in defiance of anyone who now or hereafter, by any pretense, law, or title whatever, should lay claim to the town of Mansoul. He thought, it seems, that Shaddai had no power to release them from this “covenant with death, and agreement with hell.” [Isa. 28:15] Nor did foolish Mansoul balk or hesitate at all at this monstrous pledge; as if it had been a sprat in the mouth of a whale, they swallowed it without chewing. Were they troubled at all? No; rather they bragged and boasted of their fine loyalty to the tyrant, their pretended king, swearing that they would never be turncoats, nor forsake their old lord for a new one. So Diabolus tied poor Mansoul fast.

Third. But jealousy, which never thinks itself strong enough, drove him next to another exploit: to corrupt the town of Mansoul still further, if that were possible. So he had one Mr. Filth draw up in writing an odious, nasty, lewd piece of beastliness, and had it posted on the castle gates. By it he granted license to all his true and trusty sons in Mansoul to do whatever their lustful appetites prompted, and decreed that no one was to stop, hinder, or restrain them, on pain of incurring their prince’s displeasure.
He did this for these reasons:

1. That the town of Mansoul might grow weaker and weaker, and so be less able, if tidings came that their redemption was planned, to believe it, hope for it, or consent to its truth; for reason says, the greater the sinner, the less ground there is to hope for mercy.

2. That perhaps Emmanuel, the Son of Shaddai their King, seeing the horrible and profane doings of the town of Mansoul, might repent of pursuing the covenant of their redemption, even though he had entered into it. For Diabolus knew that Shaddai was holy, and that his Son Emmanuel was holy; yes, he knew it by woeful experience, since it was for his own wickedness and sin that he had been cast down from the highest heavens. What could be more reasonable, then, than for him to conclude that it might go the same way with Mansoul, for sin? But fearing that this knot too might break, he bethought himself of another, namely:

Fourth. To try to persuade every heart in the town of Mansoul that Shaddai was raising an army to come and overthrow and utterly destroy the town. He did this to get ahead of any tidings of their deliverance that might reach their ears. “For,” he thought, “if I spread this report first, the tidings that come after will all be swallowed up in it. For what else will Mansoul say, when they hear that they are to be delivered, but that the real meaning is that Shaddai intends to destroy them?” So he summoned the whole town into the marketplace, and there, with a deceitful tongue, he addressed them like this:

“Gentlemen, and my very good friends, you are all, as you know, my lawful subjects, and men of the famous town of Mansoul. You know how I have conducted myself among you from the first day I was with you until now, and what liberty and great privileges you have enjoyed under my government, to your honor and mine, I hope, and to your delight. Now, my famous Mansoul, there is a rumor of trouble abroad, of trouble for the town of Mansoul, and I am sorry for it, for your sakes. For I have just received word by the post from my Lord Lucifer (and he usually has good intelligence) that your old King Shaddai is raising an army to come against you and destroy you root and branch. And this, O Mansoul, is why I have called you together now: to consider what is best to be done at this juncture. For my part, I am only one, and could easily shift for myself, if I cared to look after my own ease and leave my Mansoul in all the danger. But my heart is so firmly joined to you, and I am so unwilling to leave you, that I am ready to stand or fall with you, whatever risk may come to me. What do you say, O my Mansoul? Will you now desert your old friend, or do you mean to stand by me?”
Then, as one man and with one voice, they all cried out together, “Let the man die who will not!”

Then Diabolus spoke again. “It is useless for us to hope for quarter, for this King does not know how to show it. True, perhaps when he first sits down before us he will talk of mercy and pretend to it, so that he can make himself master of Mansoul again with more ease and less trouble. So whatever he says, do not believe one syllable or jot of it; for all such language is only meant to overcome us, and to make us, as we wallow in our blood, the trophies of his merciless victory. My mind, therefore, is that we resolve to resist him to the last man, and not to believe him on any terms; for that is the door our danger will come in by. Shall we be flattered out of our lives? I hope you know more of the first principles of statecraft than to let yourselves be served so pitifully.

“But suppose that if he gets us to yield, he should spare some of our lives, or the lives of some of the underlings in Mansoul: what help will that be to you who are the chief men of the town, especially you whom I have set up, whose greatness you have won by sticking faithfully to me? And suppose again that he should give quarter to every one of you: you may be sure he will bring you back into the bondage you were held in before, or a worse one, and then what good will your lives do you? Will you live in pleasure with him as you do now? No, no; you will be bound by laws that will pinch you, and made to do what you hate now. I am for you, if you are for me; and it is better to die bravely than to live like pitiful slaves. But I tell you, even the life of a slave will be counted too good for Mansoul now. Blood, blood, nothing but blood is in every blast of Shaddai’s trumpet against poor Mansoul now. I beg you, take this to heart; I hear he is coming. Up, and stand to your arms, so that while you still have some time I may teach you some feats of war. I have armor for you, here at hand; yes, enough for Mansoul from head to foot; and nothing his force can do will hurt you, if you keep it well girded and fastened about you. Come, then, to my castle, and welcome, and harness yourselves for the war. There is helmet, breastplate, sword, and shield, and whatever else will make you fight like men.

“First, my helmet, otherwise called a headpiece, is the hope of coming out well in the end, whatever sort of lives you live. This is what they had who said that they would have peace, though they walked in the wickedness of their hearts, ‘to add drunkenness to thirst.’ [Deut. 29:19] It is proven armor: whoever has it and can keep hold of it, no arrow, dart, sword, or shield can hurt him. So keep this on, my Mansoul, and you will keep off many a blow.

“Second, my breastplate is a breastplate of iron. I had it forged in my own country, and all my soldiers are armed with it. In plain language, it is a hard heart, a heart as hard as iron and as far past feeling as a stone. If you get it and keep it, mercy will not win you and judgment will not frighten you. This, then, is a piece of armor most necessary for all who hate Shaddai and would fight against him under my banner.

“Third, my sword is a tongue ‘set on fire by hell’ [James 3:6], a tongue that can bend itself to speak evil of Shaddai, his Son, his ways, and his people. Use it; it has been tried a thousand times over, and a thousand times again. Whoever has it, keeps it, and uses it as I would have him, can never be conquered by my enemy.

“Fourth, my shield is unbelief: calling into question the truth of the Word, and of all the sayings that speak of the judgment Shaddai has appointed for wicked men. Use this shield. He has made many attempts on it, and sometimes, it is true, it has been dented; but those who have written of the wars of Emmanuel against my servants have testified that ‘he could do no mighty work there because of their unbelief.’ [Mark 6:5-6] Now, to handle this weapon of mine rightly is to refuse to believe things because they are true, whatever they are and whoever asserts them. If he speaks of judgment, pay it no mind; if he speaks of mercy, pay it no mind; if he promises, if he swears that he will do Mansoul no harm but good if it turns, disregard what is said. Question the truth of it all; for that is how to wield the shield of unbelief rightly, as my servants ought to and do. And whoever does otherwise does not love me, and I count him nothing but my enemy.

“Fifth, another part or piece of my excellent armor,” said Diabolus, “is a mute and prayerless spirit, a spirit that scorns to cry for mercy. So be sure, my Mansoul, that you make use of this. What! Cry for quarter? Never do that, if you would be mine. I know you are stout men, and I am sure I have clothed you in armor of proven strength. So let crying to Shaddai for mercy be far from you. Besides all this, I have a maul, firebrands, arrows, and death, all good hand weapons, and such as will do execution.”

After he had furnished his men with armor and weapons, he addressed them in words like these. “Remember,” he said, “that I am your rightful king, and that you have taken an oath and entered into covenant to be true to me and my cause. Remember this, I say, and show yourselves stout and valiant men of Mansoul. Remember also the kindness I have always shown you, and that without your asking I have granted you outward things. The privileges, grants, immunities, profits, and honors with which I have endowed you call for loyalty in return at your hands, my lion-hearted men of Mansoul; and when will there be so fit a time to show it as when another seeks to take my rule over you into his own hands? One word more, and I am done. If we can only stand, and overcome this one shock, this one onset, I have no doubt that in a little while the whole world will be ours; and when that day comes, my true hearts, I will make you kings, princes, and captains, and what fine days we shall have then!”

Having thus armed and forearmed his servants and vassals in Mansoul against their good and lawful King Shaddai, Diabolus next doubled his guards at the gates of the town and took himself to the castle, which was his stronghold. His vassals, too, to show their goodwill and their supposed (but ignoble) gallantry, drilled in their arms every day and taught one another feats of war. They also defied their enemies and sang the praises of their tyrant, and threatened what men they would prove if things ever came so far as a war between Shaddai and their king.

Now all this time the good King, King Shaddai, was preparing to send an army to recover the town of Mansoul from under the tyranny of their pretended king Diabolus. But he thought it good at first not to send it under the hand and leadership of brave Emmanuel his Son, but under some of his servants, to test the temper of Mansoul by them first, and see whether they could win it back to obedience. The army numbered more than forty thousand, all true men, for they came from the King’s own court and were of his own choosing.

They came up to Mansoul under the command of four stout generals, each a captain of ten thousand men; and these are their names and their ensigns. The first was named Boanerges (the name means “sons of thunder”); the second, Captain Conviction; the third, Captain Judgment; and the fourth, Captain Execution. These were the captains Shaddai sent to win back Mansoul.

These four captains, as I said, the King thought fit to send to Mansoul first, to make an attempt on it; for in all his wars he generally sent these four captains in the vanguard. They were very stout, rough-hewn men, fit to break the ice and to cut their way through by force of the sword; and their men were like them.
To each of these captains the King gave a banner to be displayed, because of the goodness of his cause and because of the right he had to Mansoul.

First, to Captain Boanerges, for he was the chief, ten thousand men were given. His ensign, or standard-bearer, was Mr. Thunder. He carried the black colors, and his escutcheon, the device emblazoned on the banner, was three burning thunderbolts.

The second captain was Captain Conviction, and he too was given ten thousand men. His ensign’s name was Mr. Sorrow. He carried the pale colors, and his escutcheon was the book of the law, wide open, with a flame of fire issuing from it.
The third captain was Captain Judgment, and he was given ten thousand men. His ensign’s name was Mr. Terror. He carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was a burning fiery furnace.

The fourth captain was Captain Execution, and he was given ten thousand men. His ensign was one Mr. Justice. He also carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was a fruitless tree with an axe lying at its root.
These four captains, as I said, each had ten thousand men under his command, all loyal to the King and stout in action.

Well, on a certain day Shaddai brought the captains and their forces, their men and their junior officers, out into the field and called the roll of them all by name; and there they were fitted with armor suited to their rank and to the service they were going on for their King.

Now when the King had mustered his forces (for it is he who “musters the army for battle” [Isa. 13:4]), he gave the captains their several commissions, with a charge and command, in the hearing of all the soldiers, that they should take care to carry them out faithfully and courageously. Their commissions were the same in substance and form, though in the name, title, post, and rank of each captain there might be some very small variation. And here let me give you the sum of what they contained.
A Commission from the great Shaddai, King of Mansoul, to his trusty and noble Captain, Captain Boanerges, for making war on the town of Mansoul.

O Boanerges, one of my stout and thundering captains, over ten thousand of my valiant and faithful servants: go in my name, with this force of yours, to the miserable town of Mansoul. When you arrive, first offer them terms of peace, and command them to cast off the yoke and tyranny of the wicked Diabolus and return to me, their rightful Prince and Lord. Command them also to cleanse themselves of everything of his in the town of Mansoul, and see to it that you are fully satisfied of the truth of their obedience. When you have so commanded them (if they truly submit to it), then do everything in your power to set up a garrison for me in the famous town of Mansoul. And do not hurt the least native who moves or breathes there, if they will submit themselves to me, but treat every such one as if he were your friend or brother; for all such I love, and they shall be dear to me. And tell them that I will take a time to come to them, and to let them know that I am merciful.

But if, notwithstanding your summons and the showing of your authority, they resist, hold out against you, and rebel, then I command you to use all your skill, power, might, and force to bring them under by strength of hand. Farewell.
So you see the sum of their commissions; for, as I said before, in substance they were the same as those the rest of the noble captains had.
